analysis.one_liner: Freezes new offshore oil drilling until the Deepwater Horizon investigation is finished.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 5, 2010 and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Deepwater Horizon rig exploded and spilled millions of barrels of oil into the Gulf of Mexico, this bill would have halted new offshore oil exploration and drilling — and work on a new five-year drilling plan — until the government's joint investigation into the disaster and a report on preventing future accidents were finished. Existing producing wells would have kept operating.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, Gulf fishing and tourism communities, and taxpayers who bear the cost of oil spill cleanup and damage. A suspension gives regulators time to understand what went wrong before allowing more drilling in deep water.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gulf coast residents and fishing communities

how_it_helps.text: Suspends new exploration, development, and production activity on the outer Continental Shelf, including seismic surveys, until the joint Interior-Homeland Security investigation of the Deepwater Horizon disaster is complete [S2][S3].
Also freezes work on a new or revised five-year offshore drilling plan, unless the Interior Secretary certifies that pre-existing exploration activities pose no significant accident risk [S2][S3].
Grandfathers production that had already begun, so the bill does not shut down existing wells, only stops new activity while safety is reexamined [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to new offshore leases and drilling opportunities during the suspension, and workers on planned new drilling projects could see those projects delayed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil and gas companies and drillers

drawbacks.text: A prolonged suspension could reduce domestic oil production over time and raise prices at the pump for consumers, since roughly a quarter of U.S. oil production historically comes from the Gulf region — though the bill grandfathers existing production, cushioning the near-term effect [S2][S3].

The bill sets no deadline of its own: the freeze lasts until the investigation and a final prevention report are done, leaving the duration open-ended and creating uncertainty for coastal economies tied to drilling activity [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's cost falls on oil companies' future drilling plans, not on consumers in the short run, because existing wells keep producing. Pausing new drilling after the largest offshore spill in U.S. history is a reasonable safety step; the main design weakness is that the freeze has no fixed end date, which creates uncertainty for industry and Gulf coast workers alike.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it sat without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Nelson introduced S. 3308 on May 5, 2010, about two weeks after the Deepwater Horizon rig explosion, with four Democratic and one Independent cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action was recorded: the committee never held a markup and the full Senate never voted on the bill before the 111th Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas companies kept planning and pursuing new drilling without the suspension taking effect. The Obama administration did impose its own deepwater drilling moratorium in 2010, but this specific bill's freeze never became law, so no new statutory pause took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies pursuing new offshore drilling

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 5, 2010, to freeze new offshore drilling until the Deepwater Horizon investigation was complete.

for.name: Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Jack Reed (D-RI), Dianne Feinstein (D-CA), and Barbara Boxer (D-CA)

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Jeff Bingaman, D-NM)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Offshore drilling operators and service companies
against.what_they_did: Opposed new suspensions of offshore drilling after the Deepwater Horizon spill, arguing a freeze would cost jobs and domestic energy production.

sides.party_line_note: All five original cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's Independent (Nelson plus four Democrats and Bernie Sanders); no Republicans signed on, and the bill never advanced past committee referral.

industries.note: The bill would have frozen new exploration, development, and production on the outer Continental Shelf until the Deepwater Horizon investigation was finished, hitting future lease and drilling opportunities. Existing producing wells were grandfathered, so the near-term hit was limited to new activity. The industry's interest in keeping new drilling going runs against the coast-protection purpose of the bill, since more drilling raises the risk the bill was written to address.

Companies that conduct seismic surveys and drill new offshore wells would lose work during any suspension. Their revenue depends on new drilling activity, which the bill halts pending the accident investigation.

industries.industry: Gulf fishing, tourism, and coastal economies
industries.note: A pause on new drilling pending the accident investigation lowers the risk of another spill that could close fisheries and damage beaches — the exact harms Deepwater Horizon inflicted on these industries.
